A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same reverse-diffusion sampling work despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical results and proofs throughout, including Appendices A–C. Table 1 compares theoretical complexity bounds; no original empirical outcomes are reported.

after.justification: v3 Section 3.1 and Figures 1–2 report original Gaussian-mixture sampling experiments, including generated samples and Wasserstein-error comparisons.

M1.justification: The reverse-diffusion update and Gaussian self-normalized score estimator are retained (v1 Equations 6 and 8; v3 Equations 3 and 5). The prescribed schedule changes: v1 Theorem 3 and Appendix A.10 use nonuniform time steps and time-dependent particle counts, whereas v3 Theorem 9 specifies uniform steps and a constant particle count without target-distribution constants.

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical task coverage. v3 adds two-dimensional sampling evaluations on a 16-component, equally weighted Gaussian mixture with unit variance and a three-component mixture with unequal covariances and varying mode separation.

E2.justification: Beyond v1's theoretical comparisons, v3 actually evaluates ULA and RDMC (Huang et al., 2024a) against the proposed sampler in Figures 1–2. It also reports implementing He et al. (2024), which failed to converge, without providing a corresponding plotted curve.

E3.justification: v3 introduces empirical evaluation protocols absent from v1. Figure 2 uses step size 0.01, 500 reverse-diffusion steps and 100 score-estimation particles, with RDMC receiving a larger budget. Figure 1 instead allocates one million potential/gradient queries per method and estimates Wasserstein error from 500 generated and 500 target samples.

E4.justification: Figure 1 adds a focused sensitivity analysis of increasing mode separation at a fixed query budget, testing whether sampling error deteriorates as multimodality becomes harder. v1 contains no corresponding empirical analysis.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated experimental runs, seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests. v3's new error curves have no uncertainty bands. The analytical estimator-variance bounds are theoretical results rather than empirical uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 newly reports recovery of all 16 modes where ULA and RDMC miss modes, and substantially lower Wasserstein error as mode separation increases (Figures 2 and 1). It also reports nonconvergence of He et al. (2024). These are new empirical findings, with no corresponding v1 measurements for direct performance comparison.

T1.justification: v1's log-smoothness and forward semi-log-concavity framework, including its strong-dissipativity application, is replaced by semi-log-convexity and dissipativity assumptions. v3 introduces Gaussian-mixture guarantees, a non-Hölder counterexample, new regularity and Fisher-information bounds, and revised complexity theorems. Appendices B, D and F contain substantial new arguments; the estimator-error proof and ratio-moment analysis are retained or adapted in Appendices C and E.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes polynomial sampling under forward regularity conditions and leaves general Gaussian mixtures to future work. v3 makes coverage of all Gaussian mixtures, relaxed smoothness and operation without prior knowledge of distribution constants central contributions. It also explicitly positions novelty around guarantees for an estimator previously considered by Saremi et al. (2024).

C2.justification: v3 explains the tradeoff between weaker smoothness requirements and dissipativity, which is stronger than merely assuming a finite second moment. It substantially expands explanations of alternative score estimators and Föllmer-flow limitations, including Gaussian reweighting effects in Appendix B.1. Future-work boundaries shift from general Gaussian mixtures to distributions such as heavy-tailed targets.

D1.justification: v3 adds experimental initialization, step-count, particle-count and inner-ULA details, plus approximate local runtimes. v1 supplies theoretical parameter prescriptions only. The additions provide useful implementation information, but neither PDF supplies a code-access link or specific experimental hardware.

R1.justification: The literature discussion is substantially refocused on oracle requirements, relaxed smoothness and general Gaussian mixtures. New substantive comparisons include Chak (2024), He and Zhang (2025), and Lytras and Mertikopoulos (2025), alongside expanded Föllmer-flow and score-identity literature. v3 also explicitly acknowledges prior use of its estimator by Saremi et al. (2024).

P1.justification: v3 changes the title, extensively rewrites the abstract and introduction around three limitations, and reorganizes the main narrative into related work, results/application, algorithm and proof sketch. It replaces the earlier technical overview, restructures the appendices and adds a contents page.

P2.justification: v3 adds a Wasserstein-error plot and a three-panel sampling visualization. The earlier two-column complexity table becomes a four-column comparison covering assumptions, oracle requirements and TV complexity, and moves earlier in the narrative. The document also adopts a conference layout with revised typography and author presentation.

improvement.justification: v3 develops the Gaussian-mixture application deferred by v1, adds comparative numerical evidence and clarifies research positioning. However, the revised quantitative guarantees contain unresolved inconsistencies: Theorem 9 and Appendix F prescribe different particle-count exponents, and Table 1's TV complexity does not follow from Theorem 9's stated error/query relationship. These affect the central complexity contribution, preventing a confident net quality judgment despite the substantive additions.
